\chapter{A Clause In Front}
\label{ch:ml-participle}
\hlchaptermodality{90}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say which one I mean by putting a whole clause in front of the noun, the way Malayalam does it.}

From cold: the describing form in both tenses, the position it stands in, and the joining word English needs and Malayalam does not have.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pōkunna]{\ml{പോകുന്ന} (pōkunna) — that goes}

\label{lesson:ML-C90-participle}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{he goes}. Then say where a quality word has to stand when it describes a thing.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: take the vowel sign off the end}]
\textbf{\ml{പോകുന്നു}} is a sentence: \emph{he goes}. Take \textbf{one vowel sign} off its last letter and it stops being a sentence and becomes a \textbf{describing word}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{പോകുന്നു}} \emph{pōkunnu} & he goes — a whole sentence \\
\textbf{\ml{പോകുന്ന}} \emph{pōkunna} & \textbf{that goes}, going — describes something \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \textbf{\ml{ു}} on the final letter is gone, leaving the letter with its own built-in \emph{a}. \textbf{That is the entire change}, and it is visible on the page.

Now put it where a describing word goes — \textbf{in front}:

\textbf{\ml{പോകുന്ന} \ml{കുട്ടി}} — \emph{pōkunna kuṭṭi} — \textbf{the child who is going.}

Read that against \textbf{\ml{നല്ല} \ml{കുട്ടി}}, \emph{a good child}. \textbf{The two are built the same way.} A quality stands in front of the thing it describes; so does a verb, once it has dropped that vowel sign. \textbf{Malayalam does not need a new arrangement to let a verb describe a noun — it reuses the one you have had since the adjective chapter.}

You already produce \textbf{sixteen} of these verb forms across this book. Every one of them will do this.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pōkunnu}, then \emph{pōkunna}
  \item what came off the last letter
  \item which of the two could stand as a whole sentence
  \item \emph{pōkunna kuṭṭi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you turn a verb into a describing word? (\textbf{Take the vowel sign off its last letter}.) Where does it then stand? (\textbf{In front of the noun}.) And what else stands there? (\textbf{A quality word}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ñān vāyikkunna pustakaṁ]{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{വായിക്കുന്ന} \ml{പുസ്തകം} — the book I read}

\label{lesson:ML-C90-clause-in-front}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I read} — the sentence, with its full ending. Then take the vowel sign off the end and say what is left.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the clause goes in front, and nothing joins it}]
The last lesson put \textbf{one word} in front of a noun. \textbf{A whole clause goes in the same place.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{വായിക്കുന്ന} \ml{പുസ്തകം}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ñān vāyikkunna pustakaṁ} — \textbf{the book I read.}
\end{quote}

Line it up against English and two things are different, not one:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
English & the book \textbf{that} I read \\
Malayalam & \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{വായിക്കുന്ന}} \ml{പുസ്തകം} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The clause has moved to the front} — everything that describes the book comes before the word \emph{book}, where English trails it behind.

\textbf{And the joining word is gone entirely.} English needs \emph{that}, \emph{which} or \emph{who} to staple the clause on. \textbf{Malayalam has no such word and needs none}, because the participle is already doing that job: dropping the vowel sign is what says \emph{this verb is describing something}, and the noun that follows is what it describes.

So the thing to unlearn is the reaching-for-a-joining-word habit. \textbf{There is nothing to translate \emph{that} into.} Build the clause, drop the vowel sign, put the noun after it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{വായിക്കുന്നു}} & I read \\
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{വായിക്കുന്ന} \ml{പുസ്തകം}} & the book I read \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Only the last letter of the verb changed, and a noun arrived after it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ñān vāyikkunnu}
  \item \emph{ñān vāyikkunna pustakaṁ}
  \item which English word has no Malayalam counterpart here
  \item which side of the noun the clause sits on
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the describing clause go? (\textbf{In front of the noun}.) What word joins it on? (\textbf{None — there is no such word}.) And what marks the verb as describing? (\textbf{The missing vowel sign}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vanna]{\ml{വന്ന} (vanna) — that came}

\label{lesson:ML-C90-past-participle}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the child who is going}. Then say the past of \emph{to come} — the one form on this track that reshapes its stem.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the rule was never about the present}]
The describing form was made by taking a vowel sign off the end. \textbf{Nothing in that said which tense it had to be.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വന്നു}} \emph{vannu} & he came — a whole sentence \\
\textbf{\ml{വന്ന}} \emph{vanna} & \textbf{that came} — describes something \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \textbf{\ml{ു}} is gone, exactly as before.

\textbf{\ml{വന്ന} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ}} — \emph{vanna adhyāpakan} — \textbf{the teacher who came.}

So there are two describing forms, and the difference between them is \textbf{when}, not how:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{പോകുന്ന} \ml{കുട്ടി}} & the child who \textbf{is going} \\
\textbf{\ml{വന്ന} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ}} & the teacher who \textbf{came} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both sit in front. Both dropped a vowel sign. \textbf{Neither has a joining word.}

What gets taken off is whatever vowel sign the \textbf{last letter} carries. A past form ending in \textbf{\ml{ി}} loses that sign the same way — what is left in every case is the last letter carrying its own built-in \emph{a}. \textbf{Look at the final letter and take its vowel sign off; that is the whole operation, whatever the tense was.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vannu}, then \emph{vanna}
  \item \emph{vanna adhyāpakan}
  \item \emph{pōkunna kuṭṭi}, then \emph{vanna adhyāpakan}, and say what separates them
  \item what the operation is, in one instruction
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{vanna}? (\textbf{That came}.) What was taken off to make it? (\textbf{The vowel sign on the last letter}.) And does the rule care which tense it started from? (\textbf{No.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vishēṣaṇa vākyaṁ enna ōrmma]{(a clause in front) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R90-participle-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{he goes}, then turn it into \emph{that goes}. Do the same with \emph{he came}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one vowel sign, and a whole construction}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sentence} & \textbf{describing form} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{പോകുന്നു}} he goes & \textbf{\ml{പോകുന്ന}} that goes \\
\textbf{\ml{വന്നു}} he came & \textbf{\ml{വന്ന}} that came \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The last letter loses its vowel sign and keeps its own built-in \emph{a}.} That is the whole operation, and it does not care which tense it started from.

Then the form stands \textbf{in front of the noun}, in the position a quality word has occupied since the adjective chapter:

\textbf{\ml{പോകുന്ന} \ml{കുട്ടി}} — the child who is going. \textbf{\ml{വന്ന} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ}} — the teacher who came.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A way to say which one you mean.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{വായിക്കുന്ന} \ml{പുസ്തകം}} — the book I read.
\end{quote}

Two things differ from English, and the second is the one to watch:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
English & the book \textbf{that} I read \\
Malayalam & \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{വായിക്കുന്ന}} \ml{പുസ്തകം} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The clause moved to the front}, and \textbf{the joining word disappeared.} English needs \emph{that}, \emph{which} or \emph{who}; \textbf{Malayalam has no such word and needs none}, because the missing vowel sign already says the verb is describing, and the noun after it is what is described.

\textbf{There is nothing to translate \emph{that} into}, and reaching for one is the habit to drop. Build the clause, take the vowel sign off, put the noun after it.

This is the largest single thing the track was missing, and it turned out to cost \textbf{one vowel sign} — because the position it needed was already in use by the adjectives, and the verb forms were already in the learner's mouth.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pōkunnu} $\to$ \emph{pōkunna}
  \item \emph{vannu} $\to$ \emph{vanna}
  \item \emph{pōkunna kuṭṭi}
  \item \emph{ñān vāyikkunna pustakaṁ}
  \item which English word has nothing to correspond to it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What turns a verb into a describing form? (\textbf{Taking the vowel sign off its last letter}.) Where does the clause stand? (\textbf{In front of the noun}.) And what joins it on? (\textbf{Nothing.})
\end{tcolorbox}
